title: Checkmate in one: four patterns
outcomes: Finds a checkmate in one in the common patterns: back rank, queen next to the king, two rooks, queen with a bishop, knight
Checks every exit before calling a check checkmate
Says 'no mate' when there is none

steps.text: **Checkmate** means the king is attacked and cannot escape: there is no safe square, nothing that can capture the attacker, and no way to block it. A **mate in one** does all of that with one move. A few shapes appear again and again. The first is the **back-rank mate**.

steps.caption: The rook checks along the back rank. The king's own pawns block its escape.

line.say: The rook slides to the eighth rank. It is checkmate.

steps.text: Before you call a check mate, check every exit: can the king step anywhere, can the checking piece be captured, can the check be blocked? A back-rank mate needs the king's own pawns to stand in front of it, with no square for the king to run to.

steps.title: Same rook, one pawn moved
steps.prompt: Black's h-pawn stands on h6 instead of h7. Predict first: is there still a mate in one?

steps.caption: After Ra8+ the king simply steps to h7. A pawn move gave it a square to run to.

line.say: The king escapes to h7. It was check, not checkmate.

steps.text: Three more shapes. A **queen next to the king** is safe when your own king or another piece protects her. **Two rooks** can take turns: one holds a rank, the other gives check. A **knight's check** cannot be blocked, so it mates a king that has no square.

steps.prompt: In the last three questions you were not told whether a mate existed. How sure were you of each answer? (low / medium / high)
